items.title: EES-WIM-26-010, Water Conservation Policy Recommendations
notes:
Amy Shaw, Director of Water and Wastewater, introduced the report. Dan Meagher, Superviser of Water Efficiency, Innvoation, and Programs, spoke to the work done by staff to develop a water conservation policy recommendation. D. Meagher stated staff consulted with various groups in the community, including the Area Municipalities, 

Kirk Stinchcombe, Founder and Managing Director of Econics, explained that the Region of Waterloo is a national leader in water conservation, noting that residential water consumption is below average when compared to other municipalites in Canada. K. Stinchcombe highlighted that while the Region's water consumption is good, it can still be lower. 

K. Stinchcombe provided data to Council showing that water consumption does not peak as high over the summer months as it does in other municipalities, meaning further gains from restricting water use through bylaws would be limited.

K. Stinchcombe explained that due to the Region's existing water conservation strategies, a "step" reduction is more effective than a gradual approach. 

K. Stinchcombe explained the importance of having both immediate actions and actions on standby to be moved forward if necessary. He explained that standby actions, such as outdoor watering bans, are not immediately necessary but should be prepared in the event it's needed. 

K. Stinchcombe stated that some water conservation efforts can only be excersized by the Area Municipalities, and expressed a high level of willingness amongst these groups to participate. 

K. Stinchcombe explained that longterm actions, such as rainwater harvesting, are still effective but do not yeild short-term results. 

A. Shaw summarized the water conservation recommendations to Council, including expanding the existing conservation programs to meet demand and further incentivize water saving and revising the exisiting Water Conservation Bylaw.

Responding to a question from Council, K. Stinchcombe explained that conservation-oriented pricing can impact residents and utility companies, should be carefully considered, and is ultimately the jurisdiction of the Area Municipalities, not Regional Council.  K. Stinchcombe confirmed that this would not be feasible to implemement in 2026. 

Responding to Council, K. Stinchcombe recongnized that the Area Municipalities are already implementing many of the water conservation recommendations. 

In response to Council, K. Stinchcombe recongnized the Region of Waterloo's unique position being groundwater dependent. 

D. Meagher explained the importance of maintaing strong communications related to water conservation, as progress is very easily lost when community education is not prioritized.

Responding to Council, D. Meagher confirmed that tiered pricing has been successful in conserving water in communities outside of the Region of Waterloo. 

Committee discussed various methods of water conservation, such as tiered pricing, dual-flush toilets, and rain barrel programs. 

D. Meagher explained that rain barrel programs do not typically result in significant water savings, as only about 20% of users regularily use them. 

K. Stinchcombe explained that it is possible to incorporate household size into the water budget allocated through tiered-pricing water systems. 

K. Stinchcombe clarified that the encouragement of water source substitution at the development scales would largely need to be driven by the Area Municipalities through the development approval or planning process. K. Stinchcombe acknoweldged this is complicated by recent changes to provincial legislation. 

K. Stinchcombe emphasized that the report focuses on short-term, quick savings as opposed to long-term solutions, as this is more suitable for the Region's present needs. 

Responding to a concern from Council regarding staff capacities in Area Municipalities, A. Shaw confirmed that 10 Regional environmental officers will be available to assist with outreach, education, and enforcement throughout the Region, and Regional Bylaw officers will also be available for enforecement when needed. 

In response to a question from Council, A. Shaw clarified that funding to the Area Municipalites would be used for research opportunities and technologies and D. Meagher explained how increased funding is needed to meet the demand for the water use audit program. D. Meagher stated that the amount of audits could be doubled if the program was extended and funding provided. 

In response to Council, A. Shaw stated that there is room for improvement regarding leak detection at regional buildings, 

Responding to a question from Council, D. Meagher stated that local builders have shown interest in water conservation initiatives, but that it would be a longer process to get everyone on board due to cost. A. Shaw further explained that the costs have decreased signficantly, and will continue to decrease as the technology and availability improves. 

Staff were directed to come back to Council with information regarding re-establishing the Water Efficiency Advisory Committee.

items.title: PDL-GDS-26-013, Mannheim Service Area Water Capacity Constraint - Short-Term Growth Forecast
notes:
Rod Reiger, Commissioner of Planning, Development, and Legislative Services, introduced the report. R. Reiger explained that the report contains a short-term forecast of the Mannheim Service Area that considers demographics, economics, and federal immigration policies. R. Reiger emphasized that infrastructure constraints, such as water availability, was not considered in the forecast as the purpose is to understand true baseline demands. 

Vlad Petrov, Senior Project Coordinator from Watson and Associates, explained that various factors are negativelty impacting population growth in the Region, including N.P.R national share reductions, global economic uncetainty, and slowing housing demand. V. Petrov also hightlighted factors that positively impact population growth, such as strong Permanent Net Migration, anticipated GDP rebounds, and the Canada-Ontario Parternship to Build. 

V. Petrov explained that population growth in the Region has largely been contributed to by international migration, and as Non-Permanent Resident outflow increased, population growth has slowed. 

V. Petrov stated that the Region of Waterloo is forecasted to grow at an annual growth rate of 1.2%, reaching a population of 698,000 people by 2031. V. Petrov further stated that the Region is projected to add on average 4,100 housing units per year for the next five (5) years, which is a decrease of about 13% from what was acheived over the last decade. 

V. Petrov stated that the Manheim Service Area is expected to capture 85% of the project population increase and 83% of new housing. V. Petrov explained that there is an additional 1,200 domestic post-secondary students not captured in this data, which is estimated to bring the total number of new residents in the Mannheim Service Area to 35,700 between 2026 and 2031. 

Responding to a question from Council, R. Reiger emphasized that the Area Municipalities have been extensively consulted. 

Staff were directed to bring back a more detailed assessment on population and economic growth specific to each of the Area Municipalities.
